Volume 07 · Chapter 03

Revenue, working capital and operating cycles

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v07-c02

By the endModel operating cash needs and distinguish reported sales from cash collection.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can reconcile sales, customer collections, inventory purchases and supplier payments; distinguish a loss estimate from a writeoff; and build a dated operating-cash forecast. You can calculate a cash conversion cycle with defensible denominators and explain why it is not a complete funding forecast. Read the three-statement reconciliation and retain debit/credit, adjustment and closing conventions.

A business can report growing sales while its cash falls. Customers may pay later, stock may arrive before sale, suppliers may shorten credit, or some receivables may never be collected. These are different mechanisms. A single receivables-to-sales ratio cannot identify which occurred. Start with the transactions and their timing, then construct the ratios.

1. Revenue is a performance event; collection is a cash event

Revenue recognition determines when and how much of a customer transaction enters performance. An order is not automatically a sale; an invoice is not automatically evidence that promised goods have transferred; and a bank receipt can settle an old bill or finance work still owed. A trade receivable in our cases is an unconditional customer obligation to pay for already recognized performance. A customer advance is cash received while the specified performance remains owed.

The IFRS Foundation's public IFRS 15 overview describes a sequence of identifying the contract and distinct promises, determining and allocating the price, then recognizing revenue as control of promised goods or services transfers. Its stated effective date is annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2018, with earlier application permitted. That overview distinguishes point-in-time and over-time performance; it does not make the invoice date the recognition test.

Our simpler examples stipulate delivered, accepted goods, a fixed enforceable price and an unconditional right to payment. A pro forma invoice for an undelivered order creates neither receivable nor revenue when no payment right yet exists. A contract that creates conditional rights, multiple distinct promises, returns, rebates, disputed performance or an obligation satisfied over time needs additional analysis. Credit deterioration after a valid sale is also different from a price concession or failure to meet a contract-recognition condition. We hold the original sales recognition fixed while separately estimating credit losses; this is not a claim that every contract with doubtful collection should first be booked as full revenue.

Four entries under the chapter's explicit recognition conventions
EventEntryWhat changed?
Goods delivered on creditDr Gross receivables; Cr RevenuePerformance and a customer claim
Collect that billDr Cash; Cr Gross receivablesComposition of assets, not a second sale
Customer pays before deliveryDr Cash; Cr Customer advancesCash and an obligation
Deliver the prepaid goodsDr Customer advances; Cr RevenuePerformance releases the obligation; no new cash

Each goods delivery also transfers the supplied carrying cost from Inventory to Cost of goods sold. The selling price and that cost are different measurements. Buying stock is not necessarily an immediate expense, and paying a supplier need not coincide with either the purchase or its later sale. Inventory valuation methods, returns, taxes and complex contracts are deferred to their respective chapters rather than hidden inside a convenient ratio.

2. Gross receivables, the loss allowance and actual writeoffs

Gross receivables, G, record unpaid recognized customer claims before the loss estimate. The loss allowance, Z, is a credit-normal contra asset, deducted to obtain net receivables G−Z. It is neither cash saved in a reserve account nor a debt owed to someone else. Credit-loss expense, B, reduces profit when the estimate is recognized. In our end-balance method, evidence supplies a required ending allowance; the adjusting expense brings the existing allowance to that target.

An aging schedule groups outstanding balances by a stated status, such as days past contractual due date. Multiplying each group's gross amount by its supplied expected loss fraction gives the case's target. These fractions represent expected losses on the amount outstanding, not a forecast that every balance in a group will default. A zero-day-past-due invoice can still have credit risk. Historical averages require representative cohorts and adjustment for relevant changes; merely choosing a rate that produces desired earnings is not an estimate supported by evidence.

The IASB's May 2023 public review document, page 23, describes the IFRS 9 simplified approach for specified receivables and a provision matrix using current conditions and reasonable, supportable forecasts as well as historical experience. It is a dated explanation of requirements, not a new rule created by the review. Our supplied rates teach the reconciliation; they do not claim to estimate a real entity's compliant expected credit loss. Discounting, recoveries, grouping, enforceability and applicable framework require evidence beyond this exercise.

A writeoff removes a specified claim from the gross ledger under the supplied conclusion that it will not be recovered. Under our allowance convention, Dr Allowance / Cr Gross receivables reduces G and Z equally, leaving G−Z unchanged at that instant. It does not create another credit-loss expense for an amount already covered by the allowance. The total allowance must still be reassessed for the remaining claims; an inadequate estimate can require further expense. Removing an accounting balance is not automatically a legal release of a debtor.

For a later recovery, this laboratory uses an explicit two-step bookkeeping convention: first reinstate the recovered claim with Dr Gross receivables / Cr Allowance; then collect it with Dr Cash / Cr Gross receivables. Reinstatement alone leaves net receivables unchanged. Collection then exchanges net receivables for cash. Neither step is new sales revenue. The final allowance reassessment can change credit-loss expense; thus “no immediate expense entry on recovery” does not imply that recovery information can never affect profit. The dated MIT receivables notes supply the allowance-rollforward teaching mechanics. We do not present this posting convention as a comprehensive rule for recoveries under every current framework.

Allowance: Z₁ = Z₀ + B − W + H.
Therefore B = target Z₁ − Z₀ + W − H.

W denotes writeoffs and H recoveries that are reinstated and collected within this period; neither symbol denotes home currency here. If the required target is below the pre-adjustment allowance, B is negative: an expense reversal under the stated model. A debit pre-adjustment allowance can also occur if writeoffs outrun earlier estimates; it requires review and a supported adjustment, not a negative estimate of future losses. After adjustment our target satisfies 0 ≤ Z₁ ≤ G₁. The main case uses nonnegative ordinary balances throughout.

3. One business, all operating stocks and flows

Mesa Component Supply is a fictional trading corporation, separate from the preceding chapters' companies. The period is the 90 days from 1 January through 31 March 2025. Displayed amounts are kCU, thousands of currency units. One CU has 100 minor units, so 1 kCU is 100,000 minor units in the downloadable exact ledger. No observation about a real business is supplied.

Mesa uses the stipulated delivered-goods recognition and allowance conventions. Inventory is carried at its supplied cost; all payables relate to inventory purchases. There are no returns, discounts in the main case, inventory losses, tax, interest, depreciation, foreign exchange, acquisitions, owner movements or other balance changes. Other operating expense is paid as incurred. No contractual price changes are confused with credit losses. Ordinary collections exclude the separately identified recovery. Opening temporary accounts are zero.

Mesa opening position, 31 December 2024, kCU
Asset or contra assetAmountLiability or equityAmount
Cash30Inventory trade payables50
Gross receivables60Customer advances10
Less loss allowance(8)Contributed capital80
Inventory80Retained earnings22
Total assets162Liabilities 60 + equity 102162

The 100% estimate is maintained as an allowance at this close; the supplied writeoff decision concerns the other eight of claims already removed. An allowance amount and a decision to remove a particular gross claim are separate pieces of evidence. Required expense is 9 − 2 = 7: Dr Credit-loss expense 7 / Cr Allowance 7. Booking nine as the new expense would confuse the target stock with its required change. Net receivables are 82 − 9 = 73.

Inventory ends at 80 + 160 − 144 = 96. Trade payables end at 50 + 120 − 130 = 40. Customer advances end at 10 + 12 − 10 = 12. Revenue is 40 + 180 + 10 = 230; profit is 230 − 144 − 32 − 7 = 47. The new advance twelve is not revenue, and collecting the old claims does not repeat the credit sales.

Actual customer cash totals 40 + 150 + 12 + 2 = 204. Supplier cash totals 40 + 130 = 170, rather than purchases 160 or cost of sales 144. Direct operating cash is 204 − 170 − 32 = 2; closing cash is 32. No investing or financing cash flow is included in this quarter summary. These are grouped quarter entries, not invoice-level event dates. Their cash posting sequence never goes negative, but that fact does not establish a complete operating calendar. Purchases are stipulated to precede the related deliveries; their individual dates and cost allocations are not supplied. A different proposed cash calendar must be checked separately.

Assets grew 39, liabilities fell 8 and equity grew 47, so ΔA = ΔL + ΔE holds. Closing revenue and expenses to retained earnings changes neither those total claims nor cash. Strong recorded profit has coincided with almost no cash generation because more resources are tied up in operations.

4. Derive the cash bridge with losses included

Let Δ mean closing minus opening normal balances. Use S for total recognized revenue; G for gross receivables; Z for allowance; I for inventory; AP for inventory payables; U for customer advances; B for credit-loss expense; W for writeoffs; and H for reinstated-and-collected recoveries. Let O be the other operating expense paid currently. These identities require the case's absence of returns, price concessions, acquired balances, FX, inventory write-downs or noninventory items in AP.

G₁ = G₀ + credit sales − ordinary collections − W + H − H.
Z₁ = Z₀ + B − W + H.
U₁ = U₀ + new advances − earned advances.
I₁ = I₀ + purchases − cost of goods sold.
AP₁ = AP₀ + credit purchases − payments against payables.

The two H terms in gross receivables are deliberate: reinstatement adds the claim and collection removes it. Solving for ordinary collections, then adding cash sales, new advances and recovery cash, gives

Customer cash = S − ΔG + ΔU − W + H.
Supplier cash = cost of goods sold + ΔI − ΔAP.

Subtracting supplier cash and O, and using profit = S − cost of goods sold − O − B, produces a gross-balance reconciliation:

Define Ngross = G + I − AP − U.
CFO = profit + B − ΔNgross − W + H.

Writeoffs can shrink G without collecting cash. Omitting −W would mistake that shrinkage for cash. Recovery collection must also be included consistently with its reinstatement. In Mesa, gross operating working capital rises from 60 + 80 − 50 − 10 = 80 to 82 + 96 − 40 − 12 = 126. Thus CFO = 47 + 7 − 46 − 8 + 2 = 2.

There is an equivalent net-balance bridge. Define Nnet = (G−Z) + I − AP − U. Since ΔZ = B−W+H, substitution gives

CFO = profit − ΔNnet.

For Mesa, Nnet moves from 52 + 80 − 50 − 10 = 72 to 73 + 96 − 40 − 12 = 117: CFO = 47 − 45 = 2. The raw net-receivables change already contains the allowance change. Adding back B while also using that unadjusted net change would double-count its effect. Published reconciliations may instead adjust the working-capital movement to remove noncash items and display a separate expense addback. State exactly which movement is being used before comparing lines.

This operating N differs from current assets minus current liabilities: cash and financing debt are excluded, while customer advances are included because customers finance future performance. Its level is not “cash available.” A higher supported allowance reduces both profit and net N; it does not collect a single invoice. The NYU working-capital discussion likewise separates operating balances from cash/debt and cautions against extrapolating temporary working-capital releases indefinitely.

5. Convert stocks and flows into days carefully

The operating cycle is the sequence from obtaining inventory through selling it and collecting customer cash. Supplier credit delays the cash payment for inventory. Under steady, comparable transaction timing, the cash conversion cycle, CCC, summarizes the inventory and collection delays less supplier-payment delay. Historical statement ratios are estimates of those durations, not observations of each item's dates.

For a D-day reporting interval, choose a stated average balance. An endpoint mean, (opening + closing)/2, is available from two balance sheets but may poorly represent the path. Define the following matched-flow ratios for our case, all in days:

DSO = D × average gross receivables / credit sales.
DIO = D × average inventory at cost / cost of goods sold.
DPOcredit = D × average inventory payables / credit inventory purchases.
Operating-cycle proxy = DIO + DSO;   CCCcredit = DIO + DSO − DPOcredit.

DSO means days sales outstanding, DIO days inventory outstanding and DPO days payables outstanding. Dividing a stock in kCU by a flow in kCU per day produces days. Sales are measured at selling prices while inventory/purchases are at cost: mixing a sales denominator into inventory days changes the question. The NYU Stern ratio notes explain average-stock turnover, credit-sales matching and a purchases-based payable interval. We expose our exact denominators because not every analyst uses the same proxy.

When cash and credit sales coexist, total revenue is a convenient but different DSO denominator. Payables arise from credit purchases, so credit purchases match this ledger; a total-purchases denominator also includes purchases paid immediately. A commonly encountered COGS-based DPO proxy substitutes cost of goods sold for purchases. Even total purchases equal COGS only if inventory has not changed and there are no other inventory movements. Report the chosen definition, its data limitations and the period length rather than silently comparing unlike ratios.

Worked example 2 — Three denominators produce three different payable-day estimates

Mesa's endpoint means are gross receivables (60+82)/2 = 71, inventory (80+96)/2 = 88 and payables (50+40)/2 = 45. Over 90 days, credit sales per day are 180/90 = 2; cost of sales per day is 144/90 = 1.6; credit purchases per day are 120/90 = 4/3.

Therefore DSO = 71/2 = 35.5 days; DIO = 88/1.6 = 55 days; DPOcredit = 45/(4/3) = 33.75 days. The operating-cycle proxy is 90.5 days and CCCcredit is 56.75 days. A duration can exceed the 90-day observation window because opening stock and unfinished closing cohorts extend beyond it.

Using total purchases 160 gives DPO = 90(45)/160 = 25.3125 days. Using COGS 144 gives 28.125 days instead. The resulting CCC proxies would be 65.1875 and 62.375 days. None changes the actual supplier payment 170. They answer different aggregate measurement questions; the credit-purchase version is not an exact physical elapsed time when the inventory/receivable pools also contain cash purchases and cash sales.

Using total revenue 230 in DSO would give 90(71)/230 = 639/23 ≈ 27.783 days, not 35.5. Using average net receivables instead gives [(52+73)/2]/2 = 31.25 days. The latter changes when the loss estimate changes, even if customers' payment dates do not. Gross balances avoid that particular allowance effect, but writeoffs, changing sales rates and cohort composition can still move gross DSO.

If the relevant flow is zero, the ratio is undefined, not automatically zero days. A startup with no opening stock, a business collecting mostly cash, a seasonal inventory build, an acquisition or a change in writeoff policy may make the comparison uninformative. A 90-day flow must not be paired with 365 in the numerator unless it has first been annualized consistently. An annual convention of 360 rather than 365 is another disclosure, not a precision improvement.

6. Growth and seasonality break the shortcut from days to cash

To understand a duration interpretation, consider a deliberately steady pipeline: identical daily flows, deterministic delays, no losses, all sales and purchases on credit, constant inventory and no advances. If credit sales are s kCU per day and stay unpaid for dR days, then G = s dR: exactly that many daily cohorts remain unpaid. If daily cost of sales and purchases are c, with inventory held dI days and bills paid after dP days, I = c dI and AP = c dP. Hence

N = s dR + c(dI−dP).
CCC = dI + dR − dP.
N − c·CCC = (s−c)dR.

Even in this ideal pipeline, multiplying CCC by cost per day misses the margin embedded in receivables whenever s differs from c. For s = 3, c = 2, dI = 30, dR = 20 and dP = 40, balances are G = 60, I = 60 and AP = 80. N is 40, but CCC is ten days and c·CCC only 20. With advances or allowances, the dollar bridge needs those balances too.

For variable daily credit sales sₜ and a fixed positive integer d-day collection lag, the end-of-day gross receivable is the sum of the last d daily credit-sale cohorts, assuming older cohorts have been paid by that close. It is not generally d times today's sales or the whole quarter's average. A business selling two per day for most of a quarter and four per day just before the close can show more receivables with unchanged payment discipline. A growing closing balance divided by a lower historical sales rate can overstate the actual delay. Endpoint averaging does not eliminate that composition problem.

Negative CCC can arise when suppliers wait longer than inventory plus customer collection. It does not promise unlimited free funding, and it need not imply negative dollar N when sales contain a margin. Customer advances add another source of financing but commit the firm to future delivery or applicable refunds. Supplier terms can change, customers can delay and stock can become obsolete. A forecast needs amounts and dates as well as a summary ratio.

Worked example 3 — Same quarter totals, an interim funding gap

Consider this alternative proposed timing of Mesa's same 204 customer cash, 170 supplier cash and 32 other payments. Within each monthly bucket, assume customer receipts arrive before the listed supplier and other payments. The dates are model assumptions, not reconstructed from the endpoint balance sheets.

Unfinanced alternative cash calendar, kCU
BucketCustomer receiptsSupplier paymentsOther paymentsEnding cash from opening 30
January7080128
February546010−8
March80301032

The endpoint is still 32 and quarter CFO still 2, but February cannot finish without eight of available funding. If a zero-fee, zero-interest bridge of eight is actually available just before the shortfall, borrowing it gives balances 8, 0 and 40 before repayment. Repaying eight after March's payments restores cash 32 and leaves no closing bridge debt. These are additional gross financing flows +8 and −8; their zero net effect does not mean no financing was needed.

Without that facility or an agreed change to the payment calendar, the proposed path is infeasible under no overdraft. If supplier payments precede customer receipts inside a bucket, the peak requirement may be higher; monthly aggregation has a timing limitation. A rigorous cash forecast follows the finest economically relevant dates, distinguishes committed from hoped-for receipts and keeps facilities, fees and interest explicit.

7. Manage credit and stock without hiding their costs

Faster collections can release cash, but tighter terms may lose profitable customers. More inventory can protect service against uncertain delivery but uses funding and risks spoilage or obsolescence. Longer supplier credit may reduce immediate cash needs while sacrificing a discount, raising prices, damaging supply reliability or breaching agreed terms. Those are effects to estimate, not reasons always to minimize inventory or always to delay payment. Aging by due date, dispute status, concentration and subsequent receipts can explain more than a single DSO number.

For a supplier bill with face amount F > 0, an early-payment discount 0 ≤ d < 1 and an extra waiting time Δ > 0 days, paying early costs F(1−d). Forgoing that discount effectively pays dF for financing F(1−d) over Δ days. The interval financing rate is d/(1−d). Under a stated simple 360-day annualization, its annual equivalent is [d/(1−d)]·360/Δ. This is not an effective compound annual rate. Compare actual dated cash costs, not just the displayed percentage discount; include fees, available credit and whether the alternative loan has the same horizon.

For customer-credit decisions, separate incremental margin from expected loss, servicing cost and funding cost. A nominal sale is not a benefit if its extra collection risk and resource cost exhaust the margin. A supported allowance records an estimate; it does not itself prevent default. Improved estimates and improved cash collection are different achievements.

8. Reproduce and audit the operating model

Download Mesa's synthetic inputs, the standard-library benchmark and the README together. Run python3 v07-c03-analysis.py. Exact decimal amounts in kCU are posted as integer minor units; supplied rates and calculated day ratios use exact rational arithmetic. The default input path is relative to the script. No network or installed package is required.

The benchmark generates the case's journals, adjusts the allowance, closes temporary accounts, and reconciles gross/net receivables, inventory, payables, cash, profit and equity. It returns both CFO bridges and separately labeled cycle denominators. The alternative cash calendar reports its unfinanced shortfall and a conditional zero-cost bridge plan; it does not disguise negative cash as completed financing. The grouped ledger records stipulated performance and collections; it does not infer their detailed dates or supply documentary evidence.

For an independent reproduction, first reconstruct the three account rollforwards and cash directly from the inputs without reading the program's formulas. Then reconcile both CFO bridges. Increase only the loss target; change the mix of cash and credit purchases while holding total purchases fixed; and examine a zero denominator. Finally test the alternative calendar. Explain which results change economically, which change only through measurement, and which assumptions must be updated before a changed scenario is coherent.

Exercises

Monetary amounts are kCU; daily monetary flows are kCU per day. Assume no unlisted transactions and use the chapter's recognition, allowance and endpoint-average conventions unless a problem states otherwise. Each company or scenario is separate unless it explicitly refers to Mesa.

  1. Cutoff and collections. Amounts are kCU. On 29 June a company receives an advance of 9 for three distinct lots priced at 3 each; one lot transfers to the customer on 30 June and costs 2. A pro forma invoice for the remaining 6 creates no enforceable payment right before their July delivery. Separately, goods priced at 4 and costing 2.5 transfer on 30 June, creating an unconditional receivable payable in July. The company also collects 5 from an older receivable. With adequate inventory/receivables and no allowance change, give the June entries and combined changes in cash, revenue, cost of sales, profit, gross receivables, inventory, advances and total assets. Check ΔA = ΔL + ΔE.
  2. A second complete operating ledger. Open with cash 10, gross receivables 50, allowance 4, inventory 30, payables 20, advances 6 and contributed capital 60, with retained earnings zero. During the period: credit sales 100, cash sales 20, collections 90, all opening advances earned, new advances 8, writeoffs 5, recovery 1 through reinstatement/collection, purchases 70 all on credit, cost of sales 65, payments against payables 60 and other expense paid 15. Closing gross claims comprise 45 at a supplied 2% expected loss and 10 at 36%. Compute the allowance expense, closing position, profit, direct CFO and both gross/net working-capital bridges. Assume receipts occur before payments.
  3. Separate writeoff, recovery and re-estimation. A company opens with gross receivables 40 and allowance 5. It writes off 3, then reinstates and collects 1 of that written-off amount. There are no sales or other collections. Show gross, allowance, net receivables, cash and immediate profit effects after each step. Then set the required ending allowance at 4 and record the adjustment. Compare expense with the otherwise identical case having no recovery and the same final target; explain where the recovery's effect on final profit appears.
  4. Match the ratio to its flow. Over 120 days, gross receivables move 30→70, inventory 40→60 and inventory payables 20→40. Credit sales are 200, cash sales 100 and cost of sales 240. Purchases are 260, of which 180 are credit. There are no other movements or allowances. Using endpoint means, calculate DSO, DIO, credit-purchase DPO and CCC. Show the CCC obtained by substituting COGS in DPO, and the erroneous comparison obtained by silently substituting total sales in DSO while keeping the matched DPO. Derive supplier cash. Does any ratio recover the individual customers' payment dates?
  5. Funding is dated. A separate company has opening cash 20. It must pay suppliers 80 on day 10, receives customer cash 100 on day 30, pays suppliers 70 on day 45, receives 130 on day 70 and pays wages 20 on day 80. No other cash moves. Find the unfinanced path, quarter CFO, closing cash and minimum zero-interest credit facility needed to carry out the plan, with borrowing available before the first shortfall and repayment after the final payment. Can a facility capped at 40 suffice? Can profit be inferred from the supplied cash calendar alone?
  6. Negative days, positive funding. In the steady, all-credit, no-loss pipeline, daily sales are 5 and daily cost/purchases 2; inventory, receivable and payable delays are respectively 20, 10 and 35 days. Find the three stocks, dollar N and CCC. Increase both daily flows by 50% while keeping delays fixed; find the new stocks and additional N. Prove from N−c·CCC why a negative CCC is compatible with positive N. State why these steady comparisons still do not supply the whole transition cash calendar.
  7. The supplier's discount has a financing price. An invoice of 100 is due on day 30, or can be paid for 98 on day 10. A certain loan of 98 is available on day 10 at simple 12% annual interest using a 360-day year and is repaid on day 30, with no fees. Compare the dated costs of borrowing to take the discount and waiting. Calculate the supplier-credit interval rate and its simple annual equivalent. State the liquidity and contractual assumptions behind the cheaper choice; do not call a quoted annualization a compound return.
  8. An apparent collection improvement. Keep every Mesa transaction and gross closing balance fixed, but replace the allowance target 9 by a newly supported 15. Find expense, profit, net receivables, assets, equity, net operating N and CFO. Compare gross DSO and net-receivable DSO with baseline. Does a fall in net DSO prove that collections accelerated? Derive algebraically why increasing the allowance target by any feasible amount leaves this period's CFO unchanged when all cash events and other gross balances are held fixed.
Complete solutions

  1. Record Dr Cash 9 / Cr Advances 9. For the delivered prepaid lot, Dr Advances 3 / Cr Revenue 3 and Dr Cost of sales 2 / Cr Inventory 2. The pro forma invoice creates no June entry under the stated condition. For the separate credit delivery, Dr Gross receivables 4 / Cr Revenue 4 and Dr Cost of sales 2.5 / Cr Inventory 2.5. For collection, Dr Cash 5 / Cr Gross receivables 5.

    Cash increases 14; revenue 7; cost of sales 4.5; profit/equity 2.5; gross receivables change −1, inventory −4.5 and advances +6. Total assets change 14 − 1 − 4.5 = 8.5, equal to liabilities +6 plus equity +2.5. Neither the collection nor an invoice for unperformed goods adds revenue.

  2. Gross receivables end at 50+100−90−5+1−1 = 55. Target allowance is 45(0.02)+10(0.36) = 4.5; before adjustment it is 4−5+1 = 0, so expense is 4.5. Net receivables are 50.5. Inventory ends at 35, payables 30 and advances 8. Revenue is 100+20+6 = 126; profit is 126−65−15−4.5 = 41.5.

    Customer cash is 20+90+8+1 = 119. All purchases are credit, so supplier cash is 60; CFO is 119−60−15 = 44 and closing cash 54. Assets are 54+50.5+35 = 139.5; liabilities 30+8 = 38; equity 60+41.5 = 101.5. Opening assets 86 equal liabilities 26 plus equity 60.

    Gross N moves 50+30−20−6 = 54 to 55+35−30−8 = 52, a change −2. CFO = 41.5+4.5−(−2)−5+1 = 44. Net N moves 46+30−20−6 = 50 to 50.5+35−30−8 = 47.5, a change −2.5. CFO = 41.5−(−2.5) = 44. A working-capital release helps cash exceed profit; it is not extra sales.

  3. Initially net receivables are 35. Writeoff: Dr Allowance 3 / Cr Gross receivables 3, leaving G=37, Z=2 and net 35, with no cash or immediate profit change. Reinstatement: Dr Gross receivables 1 / Cr Allowance 1, leaving G=38, Z=3 and net 35. Collection: Dr Cash 1 / Cr Gross receivables 1, leaving G=37, Z=3 and net 34, alongside cash +1; no new revenue or immediate profit entry.

    To reach target Z=4, Dr Credit-loss expense 1 / Cr Allowance 1. Final net receivables are 33 and profit falls 1; net receivables plus recovered cash equal 34, one below their original 35. Without recovery, G would also end at 37, but pre-adjustment Z would be 2, requiring expense 2. The recovery reduces the required final expense by one in this fixed-target comparison. The estimate adjustment, not a new sale, carries that difference into final profit.

  4. Average gross receivables are 50, inventory 50 and payables 30. DSO = 120(50)/200 = 30 days. DIO = 120(50)/240 = 25 days. Matched DPO = 120(30)/180 = 20 days, so CCC = 25+30−20 = 35 days.

    The COGS proxy makes DPO 15 days and CCC 40 days. Silently using total sales 300 makes DSO 20 and, with matched DPO still 20, CCC 25 days. That ten-day difference is a denominator change, not faster customer payment. Credit supplier settlement is 20+180−40 = 160; cash purchases are 260−180 = 80; total supplier cash is 240. Equivalently, 240 COGS + inventory growth 20 − payable growth 20 = 240. None of these aggregate ratios supplies invoice-level collection dates.

  5. Unfinanced cash after the five events is −60, 40, −30, 100, 80. CFO is 100+130−80−70−20 = 60; closing cash is 80. The most negative cumulative balance is −60, so funding of 60 is necessary before day 10. Borrowing exactly 60 then produces path 0,100,30,160,140; repay 60 after day 80 to leave 80 and zero loan balance. This demonstrates sufficiency under the supplied receipt dates and zero cost.

    A limit 40 leaves a shortfall 20 on day 10. Positive quarter CFO and positive closing cash do not repair that earlier failure. Profit cannot be inferred: the receipts might collect prior sales or advances, purchases need not equal cost of sales, and other noncash expenses are unspecified.

  6. G=5(10)=50, I=2(20)=40 and AP=2(35)=70. Dollar N is 20 while CCC=20+10−35=−5 days. After the 50% increase, G=75, I=60 and AP=105, so N=30 and its increase is 10. All durations are unchanged.

    The identity N−c·CCC=(s−c)dR gives 20−2(−5)=30=(5−2)10. Receivables include the selling margin, so a negative CCC need not make the dollar sum negative. New steady balances describe the endpoints of a scale change, not the exact order in which stock is purchased, credit sales made and claims settled during the transition. Those dates still determine peak cash needs.

  7. Twenty-day loan interest is 98(0.12)(20/360)=49/75≈0.653333. Repayment is 98+49/75=7399/75≈98.653333 on day 30, versus 100 if the discount is forgone. Taking the discount saves 101/75≈1.346667 at the comparison date.

    The supplier-credit interval rate is 2/98=1/49≈2.0408% for twenty days. Simple annualization gives (1/49)(360/20)=18/49≈36.7347%, exceeding the quoted simple 12% alternative. The conclusion assumes the discount applies, the loan can actually be drawn for 98 on day 10, repayment is feasible on day 30, no fees or tax effects intervene and the supplier changes no other terms. An unavailable cheap loan cannot fund the early payment.

  8. Pre-adjustment allowance remains 2, so expense becomes 15−2=13. Profit becomes 230−144−32−13=41. Gross receivables stay 82; net becomes 67. Cash stays 32, inventory 96, liabilities 52, and assets 32+67+96=195. Retained earnings become 22+41=63 and total equity 143. Net N is 67+96−40−12=111, rising 39 from 72; CFO=41−39=2.

    Gross DSO stays 35.5 days. Net DSO becomes [(52+67)/2]/2=29.75 days, down from 31.25, despite identical actual collections. For a target increase δ, expense rises δ and profit falls δ; net N also falls δ. Thus (profit−δ)−(ΔN−δ)=profit−ΔN. The ratio movement reflects a different loss estimate, not a shorter collection calendar. The new estimate still requires its own evidence; the algebra does not validate that evidence.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain why Mesa's sales 230, purchases 160, cost of sales 144, supplier cash 170, profit 47 and operating cash 2 are all compatible. Then show why an allowance target, credit-loss expense and writeoff need not equal each other, and why a shorter reported CCC does not prove lower peak funding.

Teach-back guide

Use the inventory and payable rollforwards to obtain supplier cash, and the gross-receivable/advance/writeoff/recovery bridge to obtain customer cash 204. Target allowance 9 differs from expense 7 because pre-adjustment allowance is 2; writeoffs 8 and recovery 2 have separate roles. Net N increases 45, reconciling profit 47 to cash 2. Days require disclosed stocks, flows and averaging; a calendar with a February shortfall can share the same quarter totals. Evidence and available financing complete the interpretation.

Delayed check, after one week. Return to Mesa. Before the final allowance adjustment, write off an additional 2 of gross claims, with no extra recovery or collection. The separately supplied revised estimate still requires an ending allowance of 9. Find gross/net receivables, expense, profit, ending assets/equity, CFO and gross DSO. Explain the two steps needed to keep the same allowance target.

Delayed-check answer

Writeoffs total 10, so gross receivables end 80. Pre-adjustment allowance is 8−10+2=0, requiring expense 9 to reach 9; net receivables are 71. Profit is 45; assets 32+71+96=199 and equity 147, against liabilities 52. Net N is 115, increasing 43 from 72; CFO=45−43=2 and cash remains 32. Gross DSO is [(60+80)/2]/2=35 days. Writing off 2 first reduces gross and allowance equally without immediate net effect; replenishing the target then adds expense 2 relative to baseline. The apparent half-day DSO improvement is not a faster collection.

Sources and next steps

The inspected sources have different roles: the public IFRS 15 overview supplies the scoped recognition framework; the May 2023 IASB impairment review explains the specified loss-estimation approach; MIT's October 2003 notes support the allowance mechanics; and the Stern ratio notes and working-capital analysis motivate denominator and financing distinctions. The chapter's companies, rates, calendars and exercises are original synthetic constructions. No full subscription standard, real invoice file or current compliance conclusion is claimed.

Continue through the Volume 7 curriculum to inventory measurement, long-lived assets and the other planned accounting subjects. Their measurement choices alter the balances in these bridges. Preserving the bridge helps locate an effect; it cannot replace the recognition evidence or financing contract that gives the number its meaning.

Sources and further study

  • IFRS Foundation — IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers, public overview — Scoped explanation of contract/performance-obligation/transaction-price/allocation/control-transfer framework; effective date of 1 January 2018. Does not establish that every fictional contract satisfies every recognition condition.
  • IASB — May 2023 Request for Information: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9 Financial Instruments—Impairment — Dated explanation of expected credit losses and the specified simplified approach to trade receivables; history/current-conditions/forecast and time-value considerations in provision matrices. Not a newly enacted rule or a source for the author's invented aging percentages.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare 15.515 Financial Accounting — Midterm Review, 11 October 2003 — Dated teaching support for gross-receivable and allowance rollforwards, end-balance aging adjustment and the distinct immediate effects of writeoffs and recoveries; inventory rollforward.
  • NYU Stern course materials — Ratios (undated accessible PDF) — Inventory, receivable and payable ratio definitions; matching credit sales to receivables; purchases versus COGS proxy and cash-cycle decomposition. The chapter separately declares its credit-purchase DPO refinement.
  • Aswath Damodaran — Working capital in valuation — Operating working capital apart from cash and financing debt, unstable changes and growth forecasts, and limits on treating a negative working-capital release or supplier financing as costless and permanent.
